cells.tense: You are tending what was handed to you, and you are doing it in the open.
cells.ask: Let one thing finish this week, and when it does, let the finishing be enough — let someone say that it mattered, and receive it.
cells.core:
You are tending what was handed to you, and the pen is in your hand. Not hoarding it against the world and not letting it drift — you keep it alive and you pass it on, and you hold both cares at once without dropping either. Nothing here is forced. You tend, things grow, and you let them go when their time is done.

What you're free to feed next is the moment someone notices what you gave. Let the work be seen when it reaches its end — not as proof you were right, but as the ordinary thank-you that end makes possible. That's the next turn of the wheel, and it's already yours to take.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what was handed to you, and you tend it well.
cells.verb: Tending what's been handed down, with care that holds it together.
cells.place: Where meaning is passed between people and kept alive across time.

cells.tense: You are bracing against a future that has not arrived, trying to tend what isn't even yours yet.
cells.ask: Stop tending tomorrow's garden. Let one thing you've been carrying forward stay unfinished, and see that it survives just fine without you.
cells.core:
You are carrying the future of this thing as if it were already here. Every tradition, every practice, every handoff gets tended before it's been handed to you — and the tending has become a grip. You're keeping alive what hasn't asked to be kept alive yet, and the vigilance is costing you the ease that made the keeping possible.

The way back is to stop dreaming ahead of what you've actually lived. Let one thing finish in its own time, and when it does, trust that the finished thing carries itself. What you keep will still be there. What you've been forcing can wait.

cells.tense: You stopped tending what was handed to you, and you're still standing at the door you walked out of.
cells.ask: Pick one small piece of what was passed to you that still matters, and tend it this week — not to restore it, just to touch it with your hands again.
cells.core:
You know how to tend what was handed to you, but you've gone quiet about it. The practices are still there, the traditions haven't gone anywhere, and you've stepped back from the work of carrying them — as if the tending itself were the risk. What you carry hasn't been lost. The carrying stopped.

Returning is simpler than a return to old effort. Choose one piece of the inheritance that still breathes — a ritual, a story, a way of doing something that matters — and tend it once. Not for the future, just to see if the ground still holds you. The charge you put in comes back as strength you didn't have to force.
cells.sheetLine: You have something worth tending, and you've stopped tending it.
cells.verb: Tending what's been handed down, with care that holds it together.
cells.place: Where meaning is passed between people and kept alive across time.

cells.tense: You are already tending what matters, and you talk about it as if it were someone else's job.
cells.ask: Claim one practice, one story, one thing you keep alive for others — say out loud that you are the one keeping it, and let that be the whole sentence.
cells.core:
You are already keeping this alive. In what you repeat, in what you refuse to let go, in the quiet ways you hold a practice or a story steady — the tending is happening through you right now. But you describe it as if the work were the work, and you were just lucky enough to be standing near it. The hands are yours. You just haven't claimed them.

Start smaller than you think. Find one piece of the inheritance you've been handing to the group's name, or the family's, or the tradition's — and admit it's yours, not the ownership, the keeping. Once you say who is doing the keeping, the keeping gets easier, because the one doing it is no longer invisible to themselves.
